newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland, Hungary hail Albright's NATO stance.
newsitem.headline: Poland, Hungary hail Albright's NATO stance.

text.p: The foreign ministers of Poland and Hungary on Wednesday jointly applauded both the timetable and philosophy for NATO's enlargement set out by U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright in Brussels.

"Poland and Hungary greet with satisfaction the U.S. standpoint in the question of expanding NATO and both the calendar and the philosophy presented by Mrs Albright," said Polish minister Dariusz Rosati, summarising a joint standpoint agreed during talks with Hungary's Laszlo Kovacs.

Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic expect to be among the first former Soviet satellites to be invited, at NATO's Madrid summit in July, to start entry talks -- despite Russia's protests that an enlarged pact would threaten its security.
Rosati told reporters Albright's speech to NATO foreign ministers on Tuesday was welcome because it set out exactly what she would offer when she visited Moscow on Thursday.
"It is not forseen that Russia will be given the right of joint decision in questions that lie in the area of the prerogatives and competence of the alliance," he added.
He said the speech made clear membership talks could be completed at the end of 1997 so NATO countries could ratify enlargement in time for the April 1999 target for entry.

"Our satisfaction stems from the fact that, as expected, the offer to Russia does not contain clauses or propositions which would in any way limit the status of our future NATO membership...and will not be a formula allowing a delay in taking the decision on expanding NATO," Rosati said.
Albright suggested a new series of talks between NATO's 16 members and individual candidates for entry before July.

At the same time, NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana, due to meet Russian foreign minister Yevgeny Primakov in Brussels for talks on Sunday, also proposed a summit with Russia to seal a new relationship ahead of the Madrid gathering.
Rosati and Kovacs, who began a two-day visit to Warsaw on Tuesday, said they supported a NATO-Moscow understanding so long as it did not slow the pact's enlargement.

"We also greet with satisfaction the prospect of a NATO understanding with Russia. Poland is always a supporter of this understanding, saying that this is in the interests of Poland and all Europe," Rosati said.
Albright offered sweeteners to Russia in a speech which made clear NATO's determination to proceed with its plans.
These included an offer to create a permanent Russia-NATO brigade, which would complement NATO's vision of a joint alliance-Russia body promoting regular dialogue on security.

She added NATO countries had also agreed specific changes to the Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty, a key arms control accord, to make clear it would not take advantage of enlargement to place new forces near Russia's borders.

Rosati's summary of his joint statement with Kovacs applauded Albright's reassurance to countries which might not be in the first group of new NATO members that the pact's enlargement was an open process and would be be continued.

The two ministers, whose countries are traditional friends, said they would increase their collaboration in their shared goals of joining both the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation and the European Union.
